content:
in "The Lean Language Reference" at page :
https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#monads-and-do

there is written on class "Pure" the following :

"...
Methods

pure : {α : Type u} → α → f α

Given a : α, then pure a : f α represents an action that does nothing and returns a.

Examples:

  • (pure "hello" : Option String) = some "hello"
  • (pure "hello" : Except (Array String) String) = Except.ok "hello"
  • (pure "hello" : StateM Nat String).run 105 = ("hello", 105)
    ..."

It is wrong , as explained by tests below in VSCode :

#eval "hello" -- "hello"
#eval pure "hello" -- "hello"
#eval ((pure "hello") : Option String) -- some "hello"
#eval ((pure "hello") : Except (Array String) String) -- Except.ok "hello"
#eval ((pure "hello") : StateM Nat String).run 105 -- ("hello", 105)

the right definition should be :

Methods

pure : {α : Type u} → α → f α

Given a : α, then pure a represents an action that does nothing and returns a.
Given a : α, then pure a : f α represents an action that uses a constructor of f type and returns i a, where i a is an instance of dependent type f α.
I don't understand. What is your objection to the current docstring?

I think the load-bearing word in the existing doc is "represents". It doesn't mean the term literally evaluates to a. It means that it can be intuitively understood as an action that has no other effects
the manual says that "pure" does nothing , it is wrong because "pure a : f α" builds a dependent type instance
Could you use #backticks to format the quoted blocks of text? Using ```quote
pure a returns a whilst pure a : f α builds a dependent type instance , as witnessed by examples
pure a : f α is an action that does something , instead of nothing

GRTN said:

pure a : f α is an action that does something , instead of nothing

Can you give an example of pure a doing something?
((pure "hello") : Except (Array String) String) returns Except.ok "hello"
In this case, Except.ok "hello" is interpreted as "doing nothing" because it didn't throw a docs#Except.error, and it is interpreted as "returning "hello"" because it has "hello" inside.
you can think of it as that it succeeded in doing nothing, so you get an Except.ok because it succeeded, and then it returns a "hello"
the issue is about interpreting , a reader of a manual should understand , and to understand no more than an interpretation should be available : doing nothing doesn't mean not throwing an exception
in the Except monad, the only possible results are throwing an exception or returning ok, doing nothing doesn't throw any exceptions, so you get an ok

I'm not here to discuss if reference manual is wrong or not , the issue is that explanation of a function should be as easy as possible to understand
you can modify manual differently from what I suggested , but I found misleading original text

Maybe "side effect" is a better word to explain things? Like,

Given a : α, pure a : f α represents an action without side effects that returns a.
Of course, all of this is intuitive and there are cases that cannot be explained well with the "action" analogy
like the List monad
those are "nondeterministic actions" which return multiple values :)

yes , it is better , but returns an instance of f a not simple a

Given a : α, pure a : f α represents an action without side effects that returns f a.

...
it doesn't "return f a" because f a isn't type correct
what do you suggest ?

Aaron Liu schrieb:

those are "nondeterministic actions" which return multiple values :)

Fine, what about the FreeGroup monad :-)
I would say it returns a, in the sense that the resulting value pure a does not have a non-a value "inside" of it
I would say it returns a, in the sense that the resulting value pure a (usually) has the value a "inside" of it
yes it is , but a manual reader like me interprets that "returns a" means "hello" not Except .ok "hello"
Well, it's an action that returns a, as the manual describes

It also does nothing in that

let _ ← pure a

is a no-op
yes it is , pure a is a no-op whilst pure a : f α isn't a no-op
What is the difference between the two?

let _ ← (pure a : f α)

is also a no-op
How would a type annotation change things?
pure a returns a whilst pure a : f α returns something different from a
Oh, you're confused about the #eval behavior?
pure 3 in #eval by default is pure 3 : IO Nat
And pure 3 : IO Nat is a function that takes in a Void IO.RealWorld and returns the same Void IO.RealWorld + a result of 3 : Nat.
(although you would consider that an implementation detail)

try them on Lean :

#eval ((pure "hello") : Option String)
#eval ((pure "hello") : Except (Array String) String)
#eval ((pure "hello") : StateM Nat String).run 105

Well, I can tell that you are at least confused about the explanation in the docstring of pure. Well, I don't think the docstrings are necessarily a good resource for learning about monads; you can only really understand what pure a is once you know how monads work; and if you don't know about monads, the docstring won't help you here.

A better resource for learning about monads is probably https://lean-lang.org/functional_programming_in_lean/Monads/#monads but you can certainly find tons and tons of other resources for learning about monads elsewhere.

GRTN said:

Given a : α, then pure a : f α represents an action that uses a constructor of f type and returns i a, where i a is an instance of dependent type f α.

Well, Except.error is a type constructor too! pure a isn't just any random type constructor applied to make a f α, it's specifically the one that represents doing nothing.

pure a isn't just any random type constructor applied to make a f α, it's specifically the one that represents doing nothing.

you're right , so you can specify in the manual that it is used specifically a constructor that represents doing nothing
what would you suggest ?
It doesn't have to be a constructor though! For example, pure 3 : ReaderM Bool Nat is the function fun _ : Bool => 3
In general, I think the explanation in the docstring is correct, just not useful to anyone unfamiliar with monads.
keep explanation in the docstring unchanged

To me, it's the part "returns a" that's confusing and a bit circular, since return is just syntax for pure, and in the context of monads, "returning" often refers to a function returning (in the usual sense) a pure term.

Compare with the use of the word "return" in the documentation of SeqLeft:

Given x : f α and y : f β, x <* y runs x, then runs y, and finally returns the result of x.

In this sentence, I read "the result of x" as the inner value of type α gotten e.g. with let rx : α ← x and "returns the result of x" as then returning (in the usual sense) pure rx from the function with e.g. return rx.
